Q: Storing binary data in Google Secret Manager A:

Bypassing jq, you can use the format options built into the gcloud CLI.

gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret "my-secret" --format "value(payload.data.decode(base64).encode(base64))" | \
  base64 --decode > results.bin

Based on this similar issue here.

Q: Is it possible to parameterize table and column names in SQLite queries? A:

You cannot use a query parameter in that fashion -- to indicate a column name. You can only use it to supply values.

Consider something like this instead:

    SQLiteCommand cmd = new SQLiteCommand(
    "SELECT [ID]" +
        ",[email]" +
        ",[serializedata]" +
        ",[restrictions]" +
    " FROM " + UserTable +
    " WHERE [" + search + "] = @searchparam", SQLConnection);

    cmd.Parameters.Add(new SQLiteParameter("@searchparam"));

If you control all of the input to this function and none of it can be supplied by someone other than you, this should be safe. But if search comes from an untrusted third party, be sure to make the appropriate security checks on the value.

Q: Set timeout to http response read method in Python A:

I was wrecking my brain trying to figure this out. My problem was a server returning corrupt content and thus giving back less data than it thought it had.

I came up with a nasty solution that seems to be working properly. Here it goes:

# NOTE I directly disabling blocking is not necessary but it represents
# an important piece to the problem so I am leaving it here.
# http_response.fp._sock.socket.setblocking(0)
http_response.fp._sock.settimeout(read_timeout)
http_response.read(chunk_size)

Note: This solution also works for the Python Requests any library that implements the normal Python sockets (which should be all of them?). You just have to go a few levels deeper:

resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.socket.setblocking()
resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.settimeout(read_timeout)
resp.raw.read(chunk_size)

As of this writing, I have not tried the following but in theory it should work:

resp = requests.get(some_url, stream=True)
resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.socket.setblocking()
resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.settimeout(read_timeout)
for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size):
      # do stuff

Explanation

I stumbled upon this approach when reading this Stack Overflow question for setting a timeout on socket.recv.

At the end of the day, any http request has a socket. For the httplib that socket is located at resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.socket. The resp.raw._fp.fp._sock is a socket._fileobj (which I honestly didn't look far into), and I imagine its settimeout method internally sets it on the socket attribute.

Q: Why is there no SortedList in Java? A:

tl;dr

While this does not give you a SortedList, Java 21+ does provide Sequenced Collections. The new SequencedCollection interface lets you start with a List, then later swap out for a sorted collection such as TreeSet, without breaking related code.

SequencedCollection

Java 21 added sequenced collections to the Java Collections Framework. See JEP 431, and see talks by Stuart Marks.

Notice that List is now a sub-interface of SequencedCollection, to represent the notion that elements of the collection are iterated in a certain sequence.

SequencedCollection < String > names = List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ;

This new interface brings handy methods for accessing first/last elements, and a method to reverse the elements.

IO.println( "First: " + names.getFirst() + " | Last: " + names.getLast() ;

List sorting not maintained

That does not change the fact that the sequence of a List is arbitrary, not sorted. You can place particular elements of a list in any particular slot. As noted in the Question, if you want them sorted, you can call Collections.sort for natural order if the elements’ class implements Comparable. Otherwise, include a Comparator to do the sorting. Tip: In Java 8+, you directly call sort on the List itself rather than going through Collections utility class. Be aware that the sequence continues to be arbitrary; the sorting is not maintained as you edit the list.

List < String > names = new ArrayList<>( List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ) ;
names.sort( null ) ;  // Passing `null` rather than `Comparator` means natural-order. Sorts just this once, not continually.

names.toString(): [Alice, Bob, Carol]

If you want a List always sorted, then you must call List#sort after each and every time you insert or append elements.

Case-folding

By the way, Java 26 may bring a new feature for “case-folding”, to better support sorting with respect for uppercase/lowercase across various languages and cultures. The feature implements case-folding rules as specified by the Unicode Consortium. The case-folding works without needing to specify a particular Locale.

The String class gets a new constant, String.UNICODE_CASEFOLD_ORDER, a Comparator to implement case-folding.

names.sort( String.UNICODE_CASEFOLD_ORDER ) ;  // Uppercase/lowercase sorting per Unicode Consortium.

For more info, see JDK-8365675 Add String Unicode Case-Folding Support.

List interchangeable with SortedSet

Look at that class diagram above. Notice that SortedSet/NavigableSet, and LinkedHashSet, all implement SequencedCollection alongside List.

It is generally best to refer to your collections with the most general interface that meets the needs of your situation. If your needs are met by the interface contract promised by SequencedCollection, then use it. And if you do use it, you can later switch between any of the classes implementing SequencedCollection.

For example, you may start with a quick List such as List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ). Eventually, you realize that you want those organized alphabetically while eliminating duplicates. That qualifies their use in a SequencedSet like TreeSet. You can just switch from List to TreeSet without changing related code because TreeSet’s super-interface SequencedSet is a sub-interface of SequencedCollection.

First you write:

SequencedCollection < String > names = List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ;

Later you change the code, to swap out List for TreeSet, without breaking any related code.

SequencedCollection < String > names = new TreeSet<>( List.of( "Carol" , "Alice", "Bob" ) ) ;  // Swapped out `List` for `TreeSet` without breaking code.

If you do need a List at some point, you can easily construct one from another collection. Pass the other collection to the constructor of a list class such as ArrayList. The iteration order of the collection determines the sequence of the new List.

List < String > namesList = new ArrayList<>( names ) ;

If you want an unmodifiable List, use List.copyOf. Again, the iteration order of the collection determines the sequence of the new List.

List < String > namesList = List.copyOf( names ) ;

When creating a collection from another collection, the element objects are not copied. Only their references are copied. So relatively little memory is being used.

Choosing a sequenced collection

Here are some of the classes implementing SequencedCollection.

Class Purpose
ArrayList Hold items in arbitrary sequence. Good when usually reading or appending. Allows duplicates. Sorting possible, but not maintained.
LinkedList Hold items in arbitrary sequence. Good when often inserting/removing/swapping various elements. Allows duplicates. Sorting possible, but not maintained.
TreeSet Keeps elements in natural-order, or in Comparator order. Eliminates duplicates. Sorting maintained as you edit the collection.
ConcurrentSkipListSet Keeps elements in natural-order, or in Comparator order. Eliminates duplicates. Good for concurrent modification. Also good for rapidly adding/accessing large numbers of elements. Sorting maintained as you edit the collection.
LinkedHashSet Keeps elements in insertion-order. Eliminates duplicates.

Be aware of more classes implementing SequencedCollection, those classes implementing Deque: ArrayDeque, ConcurrentLinkedDeque, LinkedBlockingDeque, (& LinkedList).

Q: Writing data from user input via a HTA file and write it to a text file A:

As I understood, you want to write the fields names before the fields values. Like for the field values, you can concatenate strings with the & operator:

<SCRIPT Language="VBScript">
    Sub SaveData
        Set objFSO = CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject")
        If objFSO.FileExists("C:\temp\Test.txt") Then
            Set objFile = objFSO.OpenTextFile("C:\temp\Test.txt", 8)

            strLine = "username=" & UserName.Value & vbCRLF & "Email=" & Email.Value &  vbCrLf & _                 "Title=" & Title.Value & vbCRLF & "Country=" & Country.Value & vbCRLF & "Product=" & Product.Value
            objFile.WriteLine strLine
            objFile.Close
        Else
            Set objFile = objFSO.CreateTextFile("C:\temp\Test.txt")

            strLine = "username=" & UserName.Value & vbCRLF & "Email=" & Email.Value &  vbCrLf & _ 
                "Title=" & Title.Value & vbCRLF & "Country=" & Country.Value & vbCRLF & "Product=" & Product.Value
            objFile.WriteLine strLine
            objFile.Close
        End If
    End Sub
</SCRIPT>

The code could be simplified, removing the duplicated part outside the if statement:

<SCRIPT Language="VBScript">
    Sub SaveData
        Set objFSO = CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject")
        If objFSO.FileExists("C:\temp\Test.txt") Then
           Set objFile = objFSO.OpenTextFile("C:\temp\Test.txt", 8)
        Else
           Set objFile = objFSO.CreateTextFile("C:\temp\Test.txt")
        EndIf
        strLine = "username=" & UserName.Value & vbCRLF & "Email=" & Email.Value &  vbCrLf & _ 
            "Title=" & Title.Value & vbCRLF & "Country=" & Country.Value & vbCRLF & "Product=" & Product.Value
        objFile.WriteLine strLine
        objFile.Close
    End Sub
</SCRIPT>

Q: Authenticate into Apache via PHP (htaccess login done by PHP) A:

That's an interesting question because (although it's likely an XY Problem and so direct answer will be hardly useful) it gives an opportunity to understand the HTTP protocol better.

The direct answer is simple: it's not possible. PHP has no power here. Or - to put it more strictly - HTTP Basic Auth is a matter between a server and a client. So technically yes: you can authenticate PHP as a client, so PHP would be able to access these directories. But the thing is, you don't need to authenticate PHP, you need to authenticate your browser. And PHP has no power to tell a browser to become authenticated (obviously, other than sending the usual 401 challenge and so the browser would ask a user to enter the credentials, which is not the option here).

So all you can really do is to make some PHP script an index for all these directories. In this script you can check if a user is logged in and then display the listing (which takes like 3 lines of PHP code).

But there is another problem: people allowed to browse a directory usually allowed to download files and well. And here we have a problem. Once clicked on a file, the user will be prompted with the usual Basic Auth window. Which is neither your intent as well, I suppose.

So in the end, your only plausible option is to serve all listings and files fully through PHP, as explained in many existing answers - which means you don't even have to make these directories publicly accessed so they can be placed above the document root.

Q: Timeout for Python requests.get() entire response A:

I came up with a more direct solution that is admittedly ugly, but it fixes the real problem. It goes a bit like this:

resp = requests.get(some_url, stream=True)
resp.raw._fp.fp._sock.settimeout(read_timeout)

# This will load the entire response even though stream is set
content = resp.content

You can read the full explanation here.
